reason: Commission items moved from no further progress on the 2019 draft law in 2021, through repeated calls to adopt the law and strategy in 2022, 2023 and 2024, to adoption of the strategy in January 2025 and the law in June 2025, which the 2025 report counts as some progress. The chapter scale (limited progress 2021 to 2024, some progress 2025) is context only and was not decisive, and the improvement lies in the legal and strategic framework, since no item shows better coordination after the 2023 call, the 2024 audit finding of a Council that met once and the 2025 strategy's own description of coordination as critical. A February 2022 ITU item lists the law as existing while the Commission's 2022 report says it was still a draft, and later Commission and audit items support the draft reading; the differing dates for the Council (2019 or 2020) and the action plan's end (2027 or 2028) do not affect this value.

The Commission found the 2025 law sufficient for the Reform Agenda step, which required alignment of primary legislation only, yet says it does not fully align with the acquis and still asks the country to continue aligning; the law, strategy and competent authority are proposed as adopted and the by-laws and disclosure and crisis frameworks as proposed, and these statuses are themselves proposals for review. What remains is the outstanding NIS2 provisions and Cybersecurity Act certification alignment (last raised before the law passed), the 15 by-laws legally due within six months but not shown as adopted, the entity lists, the disclosure and crisis frameworks, working coordination, and application to the sectors the law defers until accession. The law's text is machine translated and capped at Medium confidence, and the regulator's one-line statement that the strategy is applied is government reporting without specifics, so neither is treated as closure.

The law and strategy, an operational competent authority and the NIS2 frameworks are each Reform Agenda payment steps, and NIS2 or cybersecurity legislation recurs in the Commission's key recommendations from 2022 to 2025. The issue is the legal base on which the rest of the cybersecurity theme rests. The rating rests on these EU requirements and not on the large number of national plan and audit items.

Much of what remains is drafting that the Ministry controls, and adoption followed within a year of the Reform Agenda step, which favours progress; against this, the first draft law stalled from 2019 to 2025, the Council barely functioned and no item shows the by-laws adopted after their deadline. Coordination needs many bodies, the strategy itself names political support and budget as key risks, and one reporting obligation to ENISA cannot be met outside the EU. Tractability is therefore higher for legal alignment than for coordination.

The Commission's wording is essentially unchanged across three reports, that state institutions need stronger capacity and infrastructure and the national centre more staff (2023, 2024, 2025), and its reform programme assessments repeat large or major deficiencies in 2025 and 2026, so the default of persistent applies; the chapter scale is context only and was not decisive. Incident counts cannot show a trend in capacity, because reporting was not mandatory and the figures are not comparable (1,441 or 1,443 for 2020, 2,804 for 2022, about 170 in 2023 on an unstated definition). The World Bank's advanced rating and the audit's finding of poor protection are a noted difference and not a conflict, since an index of national commitments and a test of practice measure different things, and the 2024 index itself lists technical and capacity measures as areas for growth.

The latest EU items, of November 2025 and April 2026, still call for significant strengthening and report major deficiencies, while responses are proposed as adopted on paper (the law, strategy and action plan, the national and government response teams) or only planned (government data centre, secure network, security operations centre), and the disaster recovery centre is used by 3 of about 140 bodies; these statuses are themselves proposals for review. What remains is staffed and trained response teams working to the Reform Agenda standard, security officers and tested plans in institutions, and secure government infrastructure in actual use. The Reform Agenda's 2024 baseline of CERTs not operational sits against statements that MKD-CIRT is in place, possibly because the baseline means NIS2 readiness, and the audit evidence behind this finding is machine translated, capped at Medium confidence, with percentages from a survey of 18 institutions.

Operational national and government CERTs, a staffed competent authority and a secure government network are Reform Agenda payment steps, and the Commission has repeated the need for capacity in its 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports. The Commission's reform programme assessments also name these deficiencies, and without operating capacity the legal framework has little effect, so the issue is central to the theme. The rating does not rest on the volume of audit and action plan items.

Progress needs people the state has struggled to hire and keep (IT posts about half filled, 3 of 11 MKD-CIRT posts filled, a shortage the strategy says extends across the region), action across about 140 bodies, and budgets the strategy itself calls at risk, while the main infrastructure is at pre-feasibility stage and looks to outside funding. Past progress is weak, as most surveyed institutions had no response team five years after the previous strategy called for them, and the new 40% salary supplement is adopted with no item yet showing its effect. Strengthening MKD-CIRT alone would be more achievable than system-wide capacity, and the audit and strategy items are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence.

The Commission has named the 5G toolbox in its recommendations in four successive reports (2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025, two of these items being classified under the framework issue), and its November 2025 wording still asks the country to continue, so the default of persistent applies; the chapter scale is context only and was not decisive. Legal steps did occur (2021 amendments, 2022 by-laws, the June 2025 law with supplier risk provisions), but the screening report says not all the 2021 amendments had been implemented. A reviewer could read the 2025 law as the start of improvement, but it began to apply only in June 2026 and no later EU item assesses it.

The latest EU items ask the country to continue implementing the toolbox, including assessing suppliers and restricting high-risk ones, and the Reform Agenda requires the security by-law fully implemented by December 2027; the 2025 law is proposed as adopted, the by-law and supplier assessment as proposed, and the 2021 amendments as reversed because the new law replaces them, all of which are proposals for review. What remains is adopting and applying the by-law and actually carrying out supplier risk assessments and any restrictions, since the law gives the power (machine translated, capped at Medium) but no item shows it used. The Reform Agenda's statement that the step is largely achieved sits against its own partial compliance baseline and the Commission's later wording, and it appears to rest mainly on spectrum and legislation, so it is not treated as closure; the Commission's finding that this law's reform step was not achieved concerns the Code and the Gigabit Act and not the toolbox, and the law allows 15 months for by-laws, so the finding does not decide this gap.

Toolbox compliance is a Reform Agenda step and has been named in the Commission's key recommendations in four successive reports, and the enlargement communication presents it as a basis of secure digital infrastructure. The issue is narrow, one clause among several in the chapter's key recommendation, so centrality is the weakest part of this rating and a reviewer could reasonably set Medium. The small number of items did not lower the rating, as volume is not a criterion.

Few actors are needed, mainly the regulator and the Ministry working with operators, the law already provides the power and by-laws under the 2021 amendments were reported adopted by the following year, which all favour progress. However, not all the 2021 amendments were implemented four years on, a supplier assessment planned from 2023 is not shown as done, and operators complained of having no consultation in 2021. The evidence does not show what restrictions would cost operators, so the rating is not set higher.

Training was mandatory for state administration bodies, but the State Audit Office reports just over 19,500 attendees by December 2023 against 129,374 public administration employees, about 15%, and calls the 73% from its survey of 18 institutions not a real picture, with no monitoring set up. The denominator is wider than the bodies obliged and the snapshot is ten months after the Conclusion, so the evidence shows real but well short uptake and not outright failure. This is a single independent audit and not government self-reporting, machine translated and capped at Medium confidence, and no later figure exists.

The audit counts attendance at the trainings that the Conclusion requires, so a contribution to attendance is plausible and direct. No baseline or start date separates attendance caused by the Conclusion from attendance that would have happened anyway, and the audit's further claim about awareness is not measured.

The State Audit Office found 13% of surveyed institutions had not taken the proposed measures, implying most had, but the same audit found 67% without two-factor authentication, which it calls a minimum measure, and no way of monitoring delivery; these two findings pull in different directions and are not resolved here. The percentages come from answers to a survey of 18 institutions, and the audit is independent and not government self-reporting, but it is machine translated and capped at Medium confidence.

The measures were recommendations, adopted five months after MKD-CIRT first published them, and there is no baseline, so institutions reporting that they took them may have acted earlier or for other reasons. The share is self-reported to the auditor by a small sample and no monitoring exists to check it.
